newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila confident of exit from IMF programme June.
newsitem.headline: Manila confident of exit from IMF programme June.

text.p: Philippine Finance Secretary Roberto De Ocampo on Wednesday expressed confidence the country would exit from the supervision of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in June despite some pending reforms.
The government is yet to complete a crucial tax reform package which has been delayed by political wranglings in the legislature.
An IMF team is currently in Manila to conduct a routine review of the Philippine economy.
The Philippines is on a three-year Extended Fund Facility programme of the IMF which is expected to end in June this year. It will be conducting another review in three months.
The review centered on the economic targets that have been met and the progress in securing vital economic reforms.
The Philippines is looking forward to its exit from 35 years of IMF guidance to improve the country's credit-worthiness and usher in more investments.

"You see we were called the sick man of Asia for such a long time and part of the reason we have the IMF around is because the sick man needs a doctor. As long as there is the sick man-doctor relationship, the image of being a sick man persisted," said De Ocampo.

"They (IMF) are satisfied and quite happy to see in many cases we have been able to exceed the targets," De Ocampo told journalists at a forum. He was referring to inflation, economic growth, fiscal and monetary targets.

"On the whole our discussions with the IMF are positive, on track and leads me to be optimistic about our capability to exit IMF within the year and most probably the original time frame we have targetted which is the end of June 1997," he said.

De Ocampo said the executive-legislative council had agreed to expedite the passage into law before May 1 the restructuring of corporate and income taxes, which are the remaining portions of the comprehensive tax reform package.
The entire package was due to be approved last year but the schedule slipped because of a controversy over taxes on beer and cigarettes.

"The non-passage of the remaining portion of the CTRP would lead to our continuation of a lousy tax system that has evolved over the years to become complicated, bureaucratic and full of instances that leads to graft and corruption. Who likes that?," De Ocampo said.
The restructuring of the income taxes would seek to reduce tax rates on individuals but shift the burden of taxes to those who can afford to pay.

De Ocampo said the Philippines has one of the lowest revenue collection rates in the region at 16 percent of gross national product versus the ASEAN average of 18 percent. The government intends to bring this up to 18 percent in 1998 and later to 20 percent, he said.
